intro: This unit follows the books of Samuel and Kings, in the part of the Tanakh called Nevi'im, the Prophets. It begins when the people of Israel ask for a king. You will meet Saul, the first king, who hid on the day he was chosen. You will meet David, a shepherd with a harp and a sling. And you will meet Solomon, who asked for wisdom and built the Temple in Jerusalem.

Then come the prophets. A prophet, or navi, is a messenger. Elijah faced a king on a mountain. Amos and Isaiah told rich people to be fair to the poor. Jonah ran away from his message and got swallowed by a fish. Jeremiah warned that Jerusalem would fall, and in 586 BCE it did. Jewish tradition still reads these stories every year: David in the Psalms, Elijah at the Seder, Jonah on Yom Kippur.

By the end of this unit you will be able to name the first three kings in order, tell the story of David and Goliath and of Nathan's lamb, explain what a prophet does, and say why Jewish communities read Jonah on the Day of Atonement. You will also be able to say what the text says and what its readers have made of it, without deciding for anyone what to believe.
bigQuestion: What do the books of Samuel, Kings and the Prophets say about power, fairness and turning back?

timeline.t: The text says Israel asks Samuel for a king; Saul is anointed
David becomes king and makes Jerusalem his capital
Solomon builds the First Temple in Jerusalem
The kingdom splits: Israel in the north, Judah in the south
Elijah speaks against King Ahab and meets the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel
Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, speaks in the northern kingdom
Isaiah begins to speak in Jerusalem
Assyria captures Samaria; the northern kingdom ends
Jeremiah warns Jerusalem that Babylon will come
Babylon burns the Temple; many people are taken into exile
Cyrus of Persia lets the exiles return to rebuild
Jonah is read on Yom Kippur; a cup is set for Elijah at the Seder

words.d: pouring oil on a person's head to show they are chosen to lead
a prophet and the last judge of Israel; he anointed Saul and David
the shepherd from Bethlehem who became the second king and made Jerusalem his capital
David's son, the third king; the text says he asked for wisdom and built the Temple
the stone house of worship in Jerusalem that the text says Solomon built
the book of 150 songs in the Ketuvim; many are headed "of David"
the Hebrew word for prophet: a person who brings a message from God
a prophet who faced King Ahab on Mount Carmel; a cup is set for him at the Seder
treating people fairly, especially those with less power; Amos's main message
turning back from wrong; the Hebrew word for being sorry and changing
the Day of Atonement, when the book of Jonah is read aloud
living far from home because you were forced to leave; the Hebrew word is galut

test.q: Who anointed both Saul and David?
test.why: Samuel, the prophet and last judge, anointed Saul in 1 Samuel 10 and David in 1 Samuel 16.

test.q: What does 1 Samuel 16:7 say the LORD looks at?
test.why: The verse says people look at the outside, but the LORD looks at the heart.

test.q: Which giant did David face with a sling?
test.why: 1 Samuel 17 tells the story of David and Goliath, the Philistine champion.

choices: Saul's son and David's loyal friend
test.why: Jonathan was King Saul's son. The text says he loved David and warned him with arrows in a field.

test.q: Why did Nathan tell David a story about a lamb?
choices: To ask for a new flock
To explain how to build the Temple
To make David see the wrong he had done
test.why: In 2 Samuel 12 Nathan's story leads David to admit, "I have sinned."

test.q: What did Solomon ask God for?
test.why: 1 Kings 3 says Solomon asked for an understanding heart, not riches or long life.

test.q: After Solomon died, what happened to the kingdom?
choices: It split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
test.why: 1 Kings 12 says the northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam. Historians date it to about 930 BCE.

choices: A prophet, a messenger from God
test.why: Navi is the Hebrew word for prophet. The Nevi'im are the Prophets, the second part of the Tanakh.

test.q: Where does 1 Kings 19 say the LORD spoke to Elijah?
test.why: The text says the LORD was not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but in a still small voice.

test.q: Which prophet's words did Martin Luther King Jr. quote about justice like water?
test.why: Dr. King quoted Amos 5:24, "let justice roll down like waters," in 1963.

test.q: What does Isaiah 1:17 tell people to do?
choices: Seek justice and defend the orphan and the widow
test.why: Isaiah 1:17 says to learn to do good, seek justice and plead for the widow and the fatherless.

test.q: What did the people of Nineveh do after Jonah's warning?
choices: They threw Jonah to a fish
They fasted, wore sackcloth and turned from evil
test.why: Jonah 3 says the whole city, even the king, turned back, and God did not destroy it.

test.q: On what day is the book of Jonah read in the synagogue?
test.why: The whole book of Jonah is read in the afternoon on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.

test.q: Who warned Jerusalem that Babylon would come, and wore a wooden yoke?
test.why: Jeremiah wore a yoke as a sign that Judah would serve Babylon. Jeremiah 27 tells it.

choices: Babylon burned the Temple and took people into exile
test.why: 2 Kings 25 tells of the burning of the Temple. Historians date it to 586 BCE. Assyria took Samaria in 722 BCE.

write.prompt: What does the Tanakh say a leader should be? Pick two or three passages from this unit, such as 1 Samuel 8:11-18, 1 Samuel 16:7, 2 Samuel 12:1-7, 1 Kings 3:5-12 or Amos 5:21-24. Say what each passage says and how Jewish tradition or another reader has read it. Then give your own answer to the question, using the text.
tips: Name each passage with its book, chapter and verse.
Say "the text says" or "Jewish tradition teaches" instead of saying whether it is true.
Use the unit's words: anointing, navi, justice, teshuvah.
Compare two readers if you can, and say how they are different, not who is right.
End with one sentence that answers the question in your own words.

title: Kings and Prophets

chapters.title: Saul, David and Solomon
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the books of Samuel and Kings say a good king should be, and what happens when kings fall short?

story.title: A Harp for a Troubled King
story.kicker: A shepherd boy walks into a palace with a harp, and the king cannot stop listening.
paragraphs: The king sat in his chair and stared at the wall. His name was Saul. He was the first king Israel ever had. He was tall and strong, but lately his mind was dark and heavy. His servants whispered. "Music might help," one said. "There is a boy in Bethlehem who plays the harp."

The boy's name was David. He was the youngest of eight brothers. He spent his days on the hills with his father's sheep. He knew how to sling a stone at a wolf. He also knew how to play a harp until the sheep lay down calm. Now a messenger stood at his door. "The king wants you," he said.

David walked into the palace with the harp on his back. He did not look at the gold or the guards. He sat down near the king and began to play. The notes were soft and slow. The king's shoulders dropped. He closed his eyes. For the first time in days, he could breathe.

The book of Samuel says Saul loved David and made him his armor-bearer. It also says that whenever the dark mood came back, David played, and the king felt better. Neither of them knew what the story would say next. One day the boy with the harp would wear the crown himself.

Jewish tradition still connects David with music. Many of the Psalms carry his name at the top. Some are sung in synagogues in Chicago every week. A song that once calmed one troubled king is still being sung.
story.think: Why do you think the story introduces David with a harp before it shows him with a sword?

lessons.title: The People Want a King
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Samuel says the people asked for a king, and Samuel warned them what a king would cost.
reading: For a long time, the book of Judges says, Israel had no king. Leaders called judges stepped up when trouble came. Then they went home. The last of these leaders was *Samuel*. He was a prophet and a judge. When Samuel grew old, the leaders of the people came to him with a request.

"Give us a king," they said, "like all the other nations." The book of *1 Samuel*, chapter 8, tells this scene. Samuel did not like the idea. The text says he prayed, and God told him to listen to the people but to warn them first.

Samuel gave a warning. A king would take their sons for his army. He would take their daughters as cooks and bakers. He would take the best of their fields and flocks. The people still said yes. Jewish tradition reads this as a story about what people give up when they want to be like everyone else.

words.d: a prophet and the last judge of Israel; he chose the first two kings
a book of the Nevi'im that tells how Israel got its first kings
a ruler who leads a whole people and passes the crown to a child

look.title: Samuel's Warning
look.text: Samuel tells the people what a king will do. He will take your sons to drive his chariots and run before him. He will take your daughters to make perfume and bake bread. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards. And one day you will cry out because of the king you chose.
look.cite: 1 Samuel 8:11-18, Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), retold in simple words
look.prompt: What is the biggest cost Samuel says a king will bring? Why do you think the people said yes anyway?

check.q: Who was the last judge of Israel before there was a king?
check.why: The book of 1 Samuel says Samuel was a prophet and the last judge. He chose the first kings.

check.q: Why did the people say they wanted a king?
choices: To be like all the other nations
check.why: In 1 Samuel 8 the people say, "like all the other nations." That is the reason the text gives.

check.q: What did Samuel warn a king would do?
choices: Take their sons, daughters, fields and flocks
check.why: Samuel's warning lists what a king would take. The people still chose a king.

lessons.title: Saul, the Tall, Shy King
lessons.mainIdea: Saul, the first king, started strong but lost his way, and the text says Samuel told him the crown would pass to another.
reading: The first king was *Saul*. The text says he was taller than anyone else in Israel. He was also shy. When the people gathered to name him king, he hid among the baggage. They had to go and find him. Samuel poured oil on his head. This is called *anointing*. It marked Saul as the one chosen to lead.

Saul won battles and gathered an army. But the book of Samuel says he made serious mistakes. Once he offered a sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel. Another time he did not do what the prophet said after a battle. The text says Samuel told him God had chosen someone else to be king.

Saul stayed king for years after that. But the story says his mood turned dark and jealous. Readers have long asked why Saul failed. Some say he cared too much about what people thought. Others say the job was simply too big for one shy man.

words.d: the first king of Israel; a tall man who hid when he was chosen
pouring oil on a person's head to show they are chosen to lead

look.title: Hiding Among the Baggage
look.text: The text says that when the people came to make Saul king, they could not find him. He was hiding among the bags and packs. When they pulled him out, he stood a head taller than everyone. Samuel said, "See whom the LORD has chosen." The crowd shouted, "Long live the king!" (1 Samuel 10:22-24, retold).
look.prompt: Why might a tall, strong man hide on the day he is made king? What does this tell you about Saul?

check.q: What does it mean to anoint someone?
choices: To write their name in a book
To pour oil on their head to show they are chosen
check.why: Samuel anointed Saul with oil. Anointing marked a person as chosen to lead.

check.q: Where did Saul hide on the day he was chosen?
choices: In a cave by the sea
check.why: 1 Samuel 10 says Saul hid among the baggage and the people had to find him.

check.q: What does the text say went wrong with Saul as king?
choices: He built the Temple too small
He did not follow what the prophet Samuel told him
He refused to lead the army
check.why: The book of Samuel says Saul offered a sacrifice himself and disobeyed after a battle. Then Samuel said the crown would pass to another.

lessons.title: The Youngest Son Is Chosen
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Samuel went to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, and God chose the youngest son, a shepherd.
reading: The text says God sent Samuel to a town called *Bethlehem*. A man named Jesse lived there with eight sons. Samuel was to anoint one of them as the next king. He did not know which one. He looked at the oldest son. He was tall and handsome. Samuel thought, surely this is the one.

The text says no. In 1 Samuel 16:7 God tells Samuel that people look at the outside, but God looks at the heart. Jesse brought seven sons past Samuel. Each time the answer was no. "Are these all your sons?" Samuel asked. "There is still the youngest," said Jesse. "He is out with the sheep."

They sent for the boy. His name was *David*. The text says he had beautiful eyes and a ruddy face. Samuel anointed him in front of his brothers. Then David went back to the sheep. Jewish tradition reads this scene as a lesson: the one who is chosen is not always the one people expect.

words.d: a small town in Judah where David grew up; his family kept sheep there
a shepherd from Bethlehem who became the second king of Israel
a person who guards and leads sheep; a picture of a good leader in the Tanakh

look.title: Looking at the Heart
look.text: for it is not as man seeth: for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
look.prompt: "Outward appearance" means what a person looks like. What does this verse say matters more? How does it fit the choice of David?

check.q: Where did David's family live?
check.why: 1 Samuel 16 says Samuel went to Bethlehem, where Jesse and his sons lived.

check.q: What was David doing when Samuel arrived?
choices: Playing the harp for the king
check.why: Jesse says the youngest son is out with the sheep. David was a shepherd.

check.q: What does 1 Samuel 16:7 say God looks at?
check.why: The verse says people look at the outside, but the LORD looks at the heart.

lessons.title: David and Goliath
lessons.mainIdea: The story of David and Goliath says a small shepherd with a sling beat a giant soldier, because he trusted and used what he knew.
reading: The Philistines were at war with Israel. They had a champion named *Goliath*. The text says he was over nine feet tall. He wore heavy bronze armor and carried a huge spear. Every day he shouted a challenge: send one man to fight me. Every day, the soldiers of Israel were afraid.

David came to the camp to bring food to his brothers. He heard Goliath. He was not a soldier, but he told Saul he would fight. Saul gave him armor. It was too big. David took it off. He picked up five smooth stones from a stream and his *sling*. He said he had fought lions and bears to protect his sheep.

Goliath laughed at the boy. The text says David told him he came in the name of the God of Israel. David ran toward the giant, whirled the sling and hit him in the forehead. Goliath fell. The story is told in 1 Samuel 17. Readers of many faiths tell it as a story about courage and using what you already know.

words.d: the giant Philistine soldier that the text says David beat with a sling
a strip of cloth or leather used to throw a stone hard and far
a people who lived on the coast and often fought Israel in the book of Samuel

look.title: Goliath by the Numbers
rows: Weight of his coat of armor in pounds (about)
look.cite: 1 Samuel 17:4-7, 16, 40, JPS Tanakh (1917); cubits and shekels turned into feet and pounds, rounded
look.prompt: David picked up five stones but used one. Why do you think the story tells us he took five?

check.q: What weapon did David use against Goliath?
check.why: 1 Samuel 17 says David chose five smooth stones and used his sling.

check.q: Why did David take off Saul's armor?
choices: It was too big and he was not used to it
check.why: The text says David had not tried the armor before and could not walk in it, so he took it off.

check.q: What had David fought before, according to the story?
choices: Lions and bears that attacked his sheep
check.why: David tells Saul he had protected his flock from a lion and a bear.

lessons.title: David and Jonathan
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Saul's son Jonathan loved David like his own soul and protected him, even though David would be king instead of him.
reading: Saul had a son named *Jonathan*. He was a brave soldier and the next in line to be king. After David beat Goliath, the text says Jonathan's soul was bound to David's soul. He gave David his own robe, his sword and his bow. They made a *covenant*, a promise to be loyal to each other.

Saul grew jealous of David. The people sang that Saul had killed thousands, but David tens of thousands. Saul tried to kill David more than once. Jonathan warned his friend. In 1 Samuel 20 they make a plan with arrows in a field. Jonathan shoots the arrows as a signal. David must run.

Jonathan chose his friend over his own chance to be king. Later, when Jonathan died in battle, David sang a sad song for him. Jewish tradition holds up this friendship as a model. The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, says a love that does not depend on getting something lasts, like the love of David and Jonathan.

words.d: Saul's son and David's closest friend in the book of Samuel
a serious promise between two sides; David and Jonathan made one to stay loyal

look.title: A Love That Lasts
look.text: Every love that depends on some thing passes away when the thing passes away. A love that does not depend on any thing never passes away. What love depended on a thing? The love of Amnon and Tamar. What love did not? The love of David and Jonathan.
look.cite: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 5:16, after Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1877), in simple words
look.prompt: What does it mean for a friendship to "not depend on a thing"? Why did the rabbis pick David and Jonathan as the example?

check.q: Who was Jonathan?
check.why: Jonathan was the son of King Saul. The text says his soul was bound to David's.

check.q: How did Jonathan warn David that Saul wanted to kill him?
choices: By sending a letter to Bethlehem
By shooting arrows as a signal in a field
By singing a song in the palace
By lighting a fire on a hill
check.why: In 1 Samuel 20, Jonathan shoots arrows and calls to his servant. The words are a signal to David to run.

check.q: What does Pirkei Avot say about the love of David and Jonathan?
choices: It ended when David became king
It was only about winning battles
It did not depend on getting anything, so it lasts
It was a love between brothers
check.why: Pirkei Avot 5:16 uses David and Jonathan as the example of a love that does not depend on a thing.

lessons.title: A City for the King
lessons.mainIdea: The text says David became king of all Israel and made Jerusalem his capital, and Jewish tradition remembers it as the City of David.
reading: After Saul died in battle, David became king. The text says he ruled first in Hebron, over the tribe of Judah, for seven years. Then all the tribes came to him. He became king of all Israel. He needed a capital city that did not belong to any one tribe.

David chose *Jerusalem*. The book of 2 Samuel says it was a hill city held by a people called the Jebusites. David captured it and made it his own. The text calls it the City of David. He brought the *Ark of the Covenant* there, the gold box that held the tablets from Sinai. The text says he danced in front of it with all his might.

David wanted to build a house for the Ark, a temple. The prophet Nathan told him that his son would build it instead. Jewish tradition remembers David as the king who made Jerusalem the center. The city is named in Jewish prayers to this day.

words.d: the hill city David made his capital; the center of Jewish prayer and memory
the gold-covered box that held the tablets from Sinai, according to the Torah
the city where the text says David first ruled, before Jerusalem

look.title: Why a New City?
look.text: Picture a map of the twelve tribes. Each tribe has its own land. David comes from Judah, in the south. The other tribes live in the north. If David rules from a city in Judah, the northern tribes may feel left out. Jerusalem sits on the border, and no tribe owned it yet. David makes it his own.
look.prompt: Why might a king choose a capital city that belongs to no single tribe? Can you think of a modern example?

check.q: Where did David rule before Jerusalem?
check.why: 2 Samuel says David ruled in Hebron for about seven years before all Israel made him king.

check.q: What did David bring into Jerusalem with dancing?
choices: The Torah scroll from the synagogue
check.why: 2 Samuel 6 says David danced before the Ark as it was carried into the city.

check.q: Who told David that his son, not he, would build the Temple?
check.why: In 2 Samuel 7, Nathan tells David that his son will build the house for God.

lessons.title: Nathan and the Poor Man's Lamb
lessons.mainIdea: The text says David did a great wrong, and the prophet Nathan used a story to make the king see it and say he had sinned.
reading: The books of Samuel do not hide David's mistakes. The worst one is in 2 Samuel 11. David saw a woman named *Bathsheba* bathing. She was married to a soldier named Uriah. David took her for himself. Then he sent orders that Uriah be placed in the front of the battle, where he was killed.

The prophet *Nathan* came to the king. He did not shout. He told a story. A rich man had many sheep. A poor man had one little lamb that he loved like a daughter. A guest came to the rich man. Instead of using his own flock, he took the poor man's lamb and cooked it.

David was furious. "That man deserves to die!" he said. Nathan answered, "Thou art the man." David understood. The text says he said, "I have sinned." Jewish tradition connects Psalm 51 to this moment. It is a psalm of *teshuvah*, turning back after doing wrong.

words.d: a prophet who told King David a story to show him his wrong
the wife of Uriah, whom David took; later the mother of Solomon
the Hebrew word for turning back after doing wrong; being sorry and changing

look.title: Thou Art the Man
look.text: And Nathan said to David: 'Thou art the man.'
look.prompt: Why did Nathan tell a story about a lamb instead of just saying what David did? What did the story make David do?

check.q: What did the rich man in Nathan's story do?
choices: Gave the poor man a hundred sheep
Took the poor man's only lamb to feed a guest
check.why: Nathan's story in 2 Samuel 12 is about a rich man who takes the one lamb a poor man loved.

check.q: What did David say when Nathan told him the story was about him?
check.why: The text says David admitted his wrong. Jewish tradition links Psalm 51 to this moment.

check.q: What does teshuvah mean?
choices: A gold box for the tablets
check.why: Teshuvah is the Hebrew word for return: being sorry and changing your way.

lessons.title: David in the Psalms and in Prayer
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition connects David with the Psalms, and some of those songs are said in synagogues every day.
reading: The book of *Psalms* is in the Ketuvim, the Writings. It has 150 songs and poems. Many have a short heading. Seventy-three say "of David." Jewish tradition calls David the sweet singer of Israel. Historians say many people wrote the psalms over many years. Both agree the songs are old and loved.

One psalm of David, Psalm 145, is said three times a day in Jewish prayer. It is called *Ashrei*, from its first word, "Happy." Psalm 23, "The LORD is my shepherd," is also read as David's. A shepherd who became a king wrote about God as a shepherd. Many readers find that fitting.

David is named in the Jewish prayer book in other ways too. A prayer after meals names the "kingdom of David." A Shabbat song says, "David, king of Israel, lives on." For Jewish tradition, David is not only a king in an old story. He is part of the words said every week.

words.d: the book of 150 songs and poems in the Ketuvim; many are headed "of David"
Psalm 145 with two extra verses, said three times a day in Jewish prayer
the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh; Psalms is the first book in it

look.title: A Shepherd's Song
look.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
look.prompt: "I shall not want" means I will not lack what I need. Why might a former shepherd picture God as a shepherd?

check.q: How many psalms carry the heading "of David"?
check.why: Of the 150 psalms, 73 have "of David" in their heading. Jewish tradition connects the book with David.

check.q: What is Ashrei?
choices: Psalm 145, said three times a day in Jewish prayer
check.why: Ashrei is the name for Psalm 145 as it is said in daily Jewish prayer, from its first word, "Happy."

check.q: In which part of the Tanakh is the book of Psalms?
choices: It is not in the Tanakh
check.why: Psalms is the first book of the Ketuvim, the third part of the Tanakh.

lessons.title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Solomon asked God for an understanding heart, and the story of two mothers shows his wisdom at work.
reading: David's son *Solomon* became king after him. The book of 1 Kings tells of a dream. God said to the young king, "Ask what I should give you." Solomon did not ask for gold or a long life. He asked for a wise heart. He wanted to judge the people well.

The text gives an example. Two women came to the king with one baby. Each said the baby was hers. There were no witnesses. Solomon called for a sword. "Cut the child in two," he said, "and give half to each." One woman said, "Yes, divide it." The other cried, "Give her the baby, only do not hurt him!"

Solomon gave the baby to the second woman. She was the real mother. She would rather lose him than see him hurt. The text says all Israel saw the king had *wisdom*. Jewish tradition also names Solomon as the author of Proverbs. That is the book of wise sayings.

words.d: David's son, the third king; the text says he asked for wisdom
knowing what is right and true, and how to act on it
the book of the Nevi'im that tells about Solomon, the Temple and the split of the kingdom

look.title: Two Mothers, One Baby
look.text: Two women stand before the king. Each says the living baby is hers. The king says: bring a sword and split the child, half to each. The first woman agrees. The second says: give him to her, only let him live. The king says: give the baby to the second woman. She is his mother. (1 Kings 3:16-27, retold).
look.prompt: The king never planned to hurt the baby. What was he really testing? What did each woman's answer show?

check.q: What did Solomon ask for in his dream?
choices: An understanding heart to judge the people
check.why: 1 Kings 3 says Solomon asked for wisdom to judge, not for riches or long life.

check.q: How did Solomon find out which woman was the baby's mother?
choices: He saw which one would give the baby up to keep him safe
check.why: The real mother would rather lose the baby than see him hurt. That is how Solomon knew.

check.q: Which book does Jewish tradition connect with Solomon's wise sayings?
check.why: Jewish tradition names Solomon as the author of Proverbs, the book of short wise sayings.

lessons.title: The Temple in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Solomon built the first Temple in Jerusalem, a stone house for the Ark, and it stood for about 400 years.
reading: Solomon did what David could not. He built the *Temple*. The book of 1 Kings, chapters 6 to 8, describes it. It was made of cut stone, lined with cedar wood from Lebanon and covered with gold inside. It took seven years to build. The Ark of the Covenant was placed in its inner room, called the Holy of Holies.

The Temple was the one place where the priests offered sacrifices. Three times a year, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, people traveled to Jerusalem to bring gifts. The text says Solomon stood before the people on the day the Temple opened. He prayed that God would hear anyone who prayed toward this house, even a stranger from far away.

Historians call this the *First Temple*. The Tanakh says the Babylonians burned it in 586 BCE. A second Temple was built later and stood until 70 CE. Today, Jewish prayers still face toward Jerusalem. Many Jewish weddings end with breaking a glass, which some explain as remembering the Temple.

words.d: the stone house of worship in Jerusalem that the text says Solomon built
the name historians give Solomon's Temple; it stood until 586 BCE
the inner room of the Temple where the Ark was kept

look.title: Solomon's Temple by the Numbers
look.cite: 1 Kings 6:2, 6:38; a cubit is about 18 inches; standing years are an approximate count from historians
look.prompt: A cubit is about a foot and a half. About how long was the Temple in feet? Was it bigger or smaller than your school gym?

check.q: Who built the First Temple, according to 1 Kings?
check.why: 1 Kings 6 says Solomon built the Temple. David had wanted to, but Nathan said his son would.

check.q: What was kept in the Holy of Holies?
check.why: The Ark was placed in the inner room of the Temple, the Holy of Holies.

check.q: About when do historians say the First Temple was destroyed?
check.why: The Babylonians burned the First Temple in 586 BCE. The Second Temple fell in 70 CE.

lessons.title: One Kingdom Becomes Two
lessons.mainIdea: After Solomon died, the text says the kingdom split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south.
reading: Solomon was famous for wisdom and wealth. But the book of 1 Kings says his building projects cost the people a lot. He used forced labor and heavy taxes. The text also says that in his old age he built altars for other gods, to please his many foreign wives. The text sees this as his great failure.

When Solomon died, his son *Rehoboam* became king. The northern tribes asked him to make their burden lighter. His young friends told him to be harsh instead. He told the people he would be harder than his father. The northern tribes walked away. They chose a man named *Jeroboam* as their own king.

From then on there were two kingdoms. *Israel* in the north had ten tribes and its capital at Samaria. *Judah* in the south kept Jerusalem and the Temple. Historians date the split to about 930 BCE. The rest of the book of Kings follows both kingdoms, and the prophets you will meet next spoke in both.

words.d: Solomon's son; the text says his harsh answer split the kingdom
the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel
here, the northern kingdom after the split, ten tribes with their capital at Samaria
the southern kingdom after the split; it kept Jerusalem and the Temple

choices: Make their work and taxes lighter
check.why: In 1 Kings 12 the people ask Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burden Solomon had put on them.

check.why: Judah, the southern kingdom, kept Jerusalem and the Temple. Israel's capital was Samaria.

check.why: Historians place the split after Solomon's death at about 930 BCE.

review.q: What warning did Samuel give when the people asked for a king?
choices: A king would make them leave Egypt
A king would take their sons, daughters and fields
A king would close the Temple
A king would end all wars
review.why: 1 Samuel 8 lists what a king would take. The people asked for one anyway.

review.q: Which is the right order of the first three kings?
review.why: Saul was first, then David, then David's son Solomon. Samuel was a prophet and judge, not a king.

review.q: What was David's job before he was anointed?
review.why: 1 Samuel 16 says David was out with the sheep when Samuel came to Bethlehem.

review.q: Which story shows Nathan using a parable to correct the king?
choices: The two mothers and one baby
review.why: Nathan tells David the story of the poor man's lamb in 2 Samuel 12. The two mothers story is about Solomon.

review.q: What did David bring into Jerusalem with dancing?
review.why: 2 Samuel 6 says David danced before the Ark as it came into the city.

review.q: Which book does Jewish tradition most connect with David?
review.why: Many psalms are headed "of David." Proverbs is connected with Solomon.

review.q: Why did the northern tribes leave Rehoboam?
choices: He moved the Temple to Samaria
He wanted to be king of Egypt
He gave the crown to Jeroboam
He refused to lighten their burden and promised to be harsher

review.q: After about 930 BCE, what was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel?
review.why: The northern kingdom made Samaria its capital. Judah in the south kept Jerusalem.

chapters.title: Elijah, Jonah and the Prophets of Justice
chapters.bigQuestion: What is a prophet in the Tanakh, and why do prophets so often say what people do not want to hear?

story.title: A Boat Going the Wrong Way
story.kicker: A prophet gets a message he does not like, so he buys a ticket in the opposite direction.
paragraphs: Jonah had a job to do, and he did not want it. The book of Jonah says the word of the LORD came to him: get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and tell them their wrongdoing has been noticed. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, a strong enemy of Israel. It lay far to the east.

So Jonah went west. He walked down to the port at Joppa. He found a ship sailing to Tarshish, about as far away as a person could go. He paid the fare. He climbed aboard. He went down below the deck and fell fast asleep. The book says he was trying to get away from the LORD.

Then a great wind came. The waves rose. The sailors were afraid. They threw cargo into the sea. Each one cried to his own god. The captain found Jonah asleep. "How can you sleep?" he shouted. "Get up and call on your God!"

The sailors cast lots to find out who had brought the storm. The lot fell on Jonah. "Who are you?" they asked. "I am a Hebrew," he said. "I worship the LORD, who made the sea and the dry land." Then he told them: throw me into the sea, and it will be calm. They did not want to. They rowed hard. The storm grew worse.

At last they threw him in. The sea went still. And the text says a great fish swallowed Jonah. He was inside it three days and three nights. Every year on Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, this whole story is read aloud in the synagogue. The story of a prophet who ran away is the story people choose to hear on the day for turning back.
story.think: Jonah runs away from a message. Why might Jewish tradition choose to read this story on the day for saying sorry?

lessons.title: A Messenger, Not a Fortune Teller
lessons.mainIdea: In the Tanakh a prophet, a navi, is a person who brings a message from God, usually one that people do not want to hear.
reading: The Hebrew word for prophet is *navi*. The second part of the Tanakh is called *Nevi'im*, the Prophets. A navi in the Tanakh is not mainly someone who tells the future. A navi is a messenger. The text often begins a prophet's speech with the words, "Thus says the LORD."

The message was often hard. Prophets told kings they were wrong. They told rich people to stop cheating the poor. They warned that a city would fall if people did not change. Kings did not like this. Some prophets were put in prison. Jeremiah was thrown into a muddy pit.

Jewish tradition counts many prophets, men and women. Miriam, Deborah and Huldah are called prophets in the text. The prophets' books in the Nevi'im come after the books of Samuel and Kings. In this chapter you will meet Elijah, Elisha, Amos, Isaiah, Jonah and Jeremiah.

words.d: the Hebrew word for prophet: a person who brings a message from God
the Prophets, the second part of the Tanakh
words that one person carries to another; what a prophet brings

look.title: Two Kinds of Prophet
look.text: Some people think a prophet is like a fortune teller who says what will happen next year. In the Tanakh, a prophet is more like a messenger who knocks on the king's door with a letter. The letter often says: you are treating people badly, and if you do not change, there will be trouble. The prophet did not write the letter and often did not want to deliver it.
look.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between a fortune teller and a messenger? Which one is a navi?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word navi mean?
check.why: Navi is the Hebrew word for prophet. The Nevi'im, the Prophets, take their name from it.

check.q: What is the main job of a prophet in the Tanakh?
choices: To bring a message, often one people do not want
check.why: A navi carries a message. The text often opens the message with "Thus says the LORD."

check.q: Which of these women is called a prophet in the Tanakh?
check.why: Deborah is called a prophet in Judges 4. Miriam and Huldah are also named as prophets.

lessons.title: Elijah on Mount Carmel
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel to show which god would answer with fire.
reading: *Elijah* was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel. The king was Ahab, and the queen was Jezebel. The text says they built altars for *Baal*, a god of the neighboring peoples. Elijah told Ahab there would be no rain for years. Then he went into hiding.

In 1 Kings 18, Elijah came back with a challenge. Meet me on *Mount Carmel*, he said. Bring the prophets of Baal. Each side would build an altar and lay a bull on it, but light no fire. The god who answered with fire would be the true God. The people agreed.

The text says the prophets of Baal shouted and danced all morning. Nothing happened. Elijah poured water over his own altar three times. Then he prayed a short prayer. Fire fell and burned up the offering, the wood and even the water. The people fell down and cried, "The LORD, He is God." Then the rain came.

words.d: a prophet in the northern kingdom who spoke against King Ahab
a god worshiped by neighboring peoples; the text says Ahab built altars for him
the mountain where the text says Elijah met the prophets of Baal

look.title: The Contest on Mount Carmel
rows: Prophets of Baal, as the text counts them
Times Elijah poured water on the altar
look.cite: 1 Kings 18:19, 18:34; 1 Kings 18:1 ("in the third year"), JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: Why do you think the story says Elijah soaked his own altar with water before he prayed?

check.q: Which king did Elijah speak against?
check.why: Elijah's story in 1 Kings is set in the reign of Ahab, king of the northern kingdom.

check.q: Where did Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal happen?
check.why: 1 Kings 18 places the contest on Mount Carmel.

check.q: What did Elijah do to his altar before he prayed?
choices: Poured water over it three times
check.why: The text says Elijah had water poured on the altar three times, and the fire still burned everything up.

lessons.title: The Still Small Voice
lessons.mainIdea: After his victory Elijah ran away afraid, and the text says God spoke to him not in wind, earthquake or fire, but in a still small voice.
reading: After Mount Carmel, Queen Jezebel promised to kill Elijah. He ran for his life. He walked into the desert and sat under a broom tree. He said he had had enough. The text says an angel brought him bread and water. Then he walked forty days to *Horeb*, another name for Mount Sinai.

There Elijah hid in a cave. In 1 Kings 19 the text says a great wind tore the mountain, but the LORD was not in the wind. Then an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. Then a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire, a still small voice.

Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak and came out. Readers have loved this scene for a long time. Many say it teaches that the most important things are often quiet. The text then tells Elijah to go back to work and to find a helper, Elisha. Later, 2 Kings 2 says Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind.

words.d: another name for Mount Sinai in the Tanakh; Elijah walked there
the quiet sound in which the text says God spoke to Elijah

look.title: Not in the Wind
look.text: and after the fire a still small voice.
look.prompt: The wind, the earthquake and the fire were loud and big. Why might the text put the voice after all of them, and make it small?

check.q: Why did Elijah run into the desert?
choices: He wanted to see the Temple
King Ahab sent him to Nineveh
Queen Jezebel promised to kill him
check.why: 1 Kings 19 says Jezebel sent a message that she would kill Elijah, and he fled.

check.q: Where did Elijah go after forty days of walking?
check.why: The text says Elijah walked forty days to Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai.

check.q: In 1 Kings 19, where does the text say the LORD was?
check.why: The text says the LORD was not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but after the fire came a still small voice.

lessons.title: Elisha Picks Up the Cloak
lessons.mainIdea: The text says Elisha took up Elijah's cloak and his work, and Jewish tradition still sets a place for Elijah at the Passover Seder.
reading: *Elisha* was a farmer plowing with oxen when Elijah threw his cloak over him. That was the call. Elisha said goodbye to his family and followed. When Elijah was taken up in the whirlwind, his cloak fell. Elisha picked it up. The text says the other prophets saw that the spirit of Elijah now rested on Elisha.

The book of 2 Kings tells many Elisha stories. He helped a poor widow whose jar of oil kept pouring until every pot was full. He healed a foreign general named Naaman, who had a skin disease, by telling him to wash in the Jordan River seven times. He warned kings and fed hungry people during a famine.

Elijah did not disappear from Jewish life. The last prophet in the Tanakh, Malachi, says Elijah will come again before a great day. So at the Passover *Seder*, many families fill a cup of wine for Elijah and open the door for him. At a baby boy's circumcision, a chair is set for Elijah. He is the guest who is always expected.

words.d: Elijah's helper and the prophet who took up his cloak and his work
the Passover meal where the story of leaving Egypt is told; many families set a cup for Elijah
a foreign general the text says Elisha healed in the Jordan River

look.title: The Open Door
look.text: It is late at the Seder table. The meal is done. Someone pours a fifth cup of wine and sets it in the middle. It is Elijah's cup. A child gets up and opens the front door. Everyone looks. No one comes in. But the cup stays full, and the door stays open a while, just in case.
look.prompt: Why do you think families set a cup for a prophet from long ago? What does an open door say to a guest?

check.q: How did Elijah call Elisha to follow him?
choices: He threw his cloak over him
check.why: 1 Kings 19 says Elijah passed by Elisha as he was plowing and cast his mantle, his cloak, on him.

check.q: What did Elisha tell Naaman to do?
choices: Wash in the Jordan River seven times
check.why: 2 Kings 5 says Naaman was healed after he washed seven times in the Jordan, as Elisha told him.

check.q: Where do many Jewish families set a cup for Elijah?
check.why: Many families pour a cup for Elijah at the Seder and open the door, because Malachi says Elijah will return.

lessons.title: Amos: Be Fair to the Poor
lessons.mainIdea: Amos, a shepherd from the south, said that worship means nothing if people cheat the poor; the text says justice should flow like water.
reading: *Amos* was a shepherd and a keeper of fig trees from Tekoa, a village in Judah. The text says God sent him north to Israel, around 750 BCE. It was a rich time there. Big houses, fancy feasts, full markets. But Amos said the rich were cheating the poor, using false weights and selling people into slavery for the price of a pair of shoes.

Amos went to Bethel, a shrine in the north, and spoke. He said God did not want their festivals and songs. He wanted fairness. The book of Amos 5:24 says: let *justice* well up like water, and righteousness like a strong stream. A priest at Bethel told Amos to go home. Amos said he was not a professional prophet. He was just a shepherd who was sent.

Amos is one of the Twelve, the short prophetic books at the end of the Nevi'im. Many readers have used his words. In 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. quoted Amos 5:24 in his "I Have a Dream" speech. Jewish tradition reads Amos as a reminder that prayer and fair dealing belong together.

words.d: a shepherd from Tekoa whom the text says God sent to speak against cheating the poor
treating people fairly, especially those with less power
twelve short books of prophets at the end of the Nevi'im, kept on one scroll

look.title: Justice Like Water
look.text: But let justice well up as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
look.prompt: Water in a stream keeps moving and reaches everyone downstream. Why is that a good picture for justice?

check.q: What was Amos's job before he was a prophet?
choices: A shepherd and keeper of fig trees
check.why: Amos 7:14 says Amos was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore fig trees.

check.q: What did Amos say was wrong in the northern kingdom?
choices: The rich were cheating the poor
check.why: Amos says the rich used false weights and sold the poor for the price of shoes. God wants justice, not just festivals.

check.q: Who quoted Amos 5:24 in a famous speech in 1963?
check.why: Dr. King quoted "let justice roll down like waters" in his "I Have a Dream" speech in 1963.

lessons.title: Isaiah in Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah spoke in Jerusalem and said the same thing as Amos: care for the orphan and widow, and a day will come when swords become plows.
reading: *Isaiah* lived in Jerusalem, in the kingdom of Judah. He spoke a little after Amos. The text says he saw a vision of God in the Temple. Angels called, "Holy, holy, holy." He spoke to kings for about forty years. His book is the first of the big prophetic books in the Nevi'im.

Like Amos, Isaiah said offerings meant nothing without fairness. Isaiah 1:17 says to learn to do good and seek justice. Help the oppressed. Defend the *orphan*. Plead for the *widow*. In his time, an orphan or a widow had no one to stand up for them. Isaiah said a city is judged by how it treats them.

Isaiah is also known for a picture of peace. Isaiah 2:4 says nations will beat their swords into plowshares. A plowshare is the blade that cuts soil. They will not learn war anymore. Those words are carved on a wall across from the United Nations in New York. Jewish readers hear Isaiah every year in the haftarah. That is the reading from the Prophets after the Torah portion.

words.d: a prophet in Jerusalem whose book is the first of the big prophetic books
a child whose parents have died; the prophets say to protect them
a woman whose husband has died; the prophets say to defend her
the reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading in the synagogue

look.title: Swords into Plowshares
look.text: Isaiah says that in days to come, nations will hammer their swords into plow blades and their spears into pruning knives. Nation will not lift up sword against nation, and they will not learn war anymore.
look.cite: Isaiah 2:4, Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), in simple words
look.prompt: A plowshare grows food and a sword hurts people. What is Isaiah saying the nations will do with their weapons?

check.q: Where did Isaiah live and speak?
check.why: Isaiah was a prophet in Jerusalem, the capital of the southern kingdom of Judah.

check.q: According to Isaiah 1:17, whom should people defend?
check.why: Isaiah 1:17 says to judge the fatherless and plead for the widow, the people with no one to stand up for them.

check.q: What does Isaiah 2:4 say will happen to swords?
choices: They will be buried under the Temple
They will be given to the king
They will be beaten into plowshares
They will be thrown into the sea
check.why: Isaiah 2:4 pictures nations turning weapons into farm tools and not learning war anymore.

lessons.title: A Prophet Runs Away
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Jonah says a prophet ran from his message, was swallowed by a great fish and prayed from inside it.
reading: The book of *Jonah* is one of the Twelve. It is only four chapters long. It is different from the other prophets' books. Instead of long speeches, it tells a story. Jonah is told to go to *Nineveh* and warn it. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that later destroyed the northern kingdom. Jonah goes the other way.

A storm hits the ship. The sailors throw Jonah into the sea, and it goes calm. The text says a great fish swallows him. Inside the fish, Jonah prays. His prayer in chapter 2 sounds like a psalm. He says he called out from the belly of the deep, and God heard him. After three days the fish spits him out onto dry land.

Readers of all ages have argued about the fish. Was it a whale? The Hebrew says only "a great fish." Jewish tradition usually reads the story for what it teaches, not for the zoology. The point, many say, is that you cannot run away from a job you are meant to do, and that a person can pray from anywhere, even from inside a fish.

words.d: a prophet in one of the Twelve who ran from his message and was swallowed by a great fish
the capital of Assyria; the city Jonah was sent to warn
the faraway port Jonah tried to sail to, in the opposite direction from Nineveh

look.title: Jonah by the Numbers
rows: Chapters in the book of Jonah
Days and nights inside the fish
Days Jonah gave Nineveh to change
People in Nineveh, as the text counts (thousands)
look.prompt: The text gives Nineveh forty days. Where else in the Tanakh have you seen the number forty? What might it mean here?

check.q: Which direction did Jonah go when told to go to Nineveh?
check.why: Jonah went down to Joppa and took a ship for Tarshish, away from Nineveh.

check.q: What did Jonah do inside the fish?
choices: He wrote a letter to the king
check.why: Jonah chapter 2 is a prayer from inside the fish. It sounds like a psalm.

check.q: What city was Jonah sent to warn?
check.why: Jonah 1:2 says to go to Nineveh, the great city, the capital of Assyria.

lessons.title: Nineveh Says Sorry
lessons.mainIdea: The text says all of Nineveh, from the king down, turned back from evil, and Jonah was angry that God forgave them.
reading: Jonah finally goes to Nineveh. He walks into the huge city and says just five words in Hebrew: in forty days, Nineveh will be overturned. Then something surprising happens. The people believe him. They stop eating. They put on rough cloth called sackcloth. Even the king gets off his throne and sits in ashes.

The king orders everyone, even the animals, to fast. He says, let everyone turn from their evil ways and from the violence in their hands. Who knows, he says, maybe God will turn back too. The text says God saw what they did, not what they said, and did not destroy the city. This is *teshuvah*: turning back.

Jonah is furious. He sits outside the city and sulks. God makes a plant grow to shade him, then lets a worm kill it. Jonah is upset about the plant. The book ends with a question from God: you cared about a plant you did not grow; should I not care about a city of more than 120,000 people, and many animals too? Jonah never answers. The reader has to.

words.d: rough, scratchy cloth people in the Tanakh wore to show they were sorry
turning back from wrong; the Hebrew word for being sorry and changing
to go without food for a time, often as a way of saying sorry or praying

look.title: The Last Question
look.text: The book of Jonah ends with God asking Jonah a question. Jonah was sad about a plant that grew in one night and died in one night. God asks: should I not care about Nineveh, a great city with more than 120,000 people who do not know their right hand from their left, and many animals? (Jonah 4:10-11, retold). The book stops there. Jonah does not answer.
look.prompt: Why do you think the book ends with a question and no answer? What would you say back if you were Jonah?

check.q: What did the people of Nineveh do when they heard Jonah?
choices: They threw him in the river
They fasted, wore sackcloth and turned from evil
check.why: Jonah 3 says the people believed, fasted and put on sackcloth, and even the king sat in ashes.

check.q: How did Jonah feel when God did not destroy Nineveh?
check.why: Jonah 4 says Jonah was very angry that God forgave the city.

check.q: How does the book of Jonah end?
choices: With a question from God that Jonah does not answer
With Jonah becoming king of Nineveh
With the fish swallowing Jonah again
check.why: The last verse is God's question about caring for Nineveh. The book gives no answer.

lessons.title: Jonah on Yom Kippur
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish communities read the whole book of Jonah on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, because it is a story about turning back.
reading: *Yom Kippur* is the Day of Atonement. It comes ten days after the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah. Jewish tradition treats it as the most serious day of the year. Many Jewish adults fast from sunset to sunset. People spend the day in the synagogue, saying sorry for wrongs and asking to be forgiven.

In the afternoon service, the whole book of Jonah is read aloud as the haftarah. It is a strange choice at first. Jonah is a prophet who does everything wrong. But the people of Nineveh, who are not even Israelites, do everything right. They hear a warning, they turn back, and they are forgiven.

Rabbis over the centuries have explained the choice in many ways. Some say it shows that no one can run from God. Some say it shows that saying sorry really works, for anyone. Some point to the last line: God cares for every person and even the animals. On the day for teshuvah, Jewish tradition reads the story of a whole city that did it.

words.d: the Day of Atonement, the most serious day of the Jewish year; many adults fast
the Jewish New Year, ten days before Yom Kippur
making things right after doing wrong; being forgiven

look.title: Why This Story Today?
look.text: It is late afternoon on Yom Kippur in a Chicago synagogue. People have not eaten since last night. The reader opens the book of Jonah and chants it, all four chapters. The congregation hears about the ship, the fish, the city that turned back, and the plant. Then comes the last question, and the reader stops.
look.prompt: Imagine you are choosing one story to read on the day for saying sorry. Why would Jonah be a good choice? Why might it be a hard choice?

check.q: When is the book of Jonah read aloud in the synagogue?
choices: On Yom Kippur, in the afternoon
check.why: Jewish tradition reads the whole book of Jonah as the afternoon haftarah on Yom Kippur.

check.q: What is Yom Kippur?
choices: The festival of the Torah's giving
The Day of Atonement, a day for saying sorry and being forgiven
check.why: Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement. Rosh Hashanah is the New Year, ten days earlier.

check.q: Why does the book of Jonah fit Yom Kippur, according to many rabbis?
choices: It shows a whole city turning back and being forgiven
check.why: Nineveh hears a warning, turns from evil and is forgiven. That is teshuvah, the theme of Yom Kippur.

sections.title: Jeremiah and the Fall of Jerusalem

lessons.title: Jeremiah Warns the City
lessons.mainIdea: Jeremiah told Jerusalem that Babylon would come, and the text says people put him in a pit for saying it.
reading: *Jeremiah* was a prophet in Jerusalem about 150 years after Isaiah. By then the northern kingdom was gone. Assyria had taken Samaria in 722 BCE. Now a new empire, *Babylon*, was growing in the east. Jeremiah said Babylon would take Jerusalem too, unless the people changed how they lived.

Nobody wanted to hear it. Jeremiah stood at the Temple gate and said the building would not save them. Only doing justice would. He wore a wooden yoke, the bar that goes over an ox's neck, to show that Judah would serve Babylon. Priests and officials were angry. The text says they beat him and lowered him into a muddy pit.

Jeremiah's book shows his feelings more than most. He says he wished he had never been born. He says the message burned inside him like a fire, and he could not hold it in. Jewish tradition also connects Jeremiah with the book of *Lamentations*, the sad poems for the burned city.

words.d: a prophet in Jerusalem who warned that Babylon would take the city
the empire in the east that the text says burned Jerusalem in 586 BCE
a short book of sad poems for the fall of Jerusalem; tradition connects it with Jeremiah

look.title: A Fire Inside
look.text: Jeremiah says that when he decided not to speak in God's name anymore, the word became like a burning fire shut up in his bones. He grew tired of holding it in, and he could not.
look.cite: Jeremiah 20:9, Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917), in simple words
look.prompt: Have you ever had something you felt you had to say? How does Jeremiah describe what it feels like to hold a message in?

check.q: What did Jeremiah say would happen to Jerusalem?
choices: Babylon would take it unless the people changed
Egypt would make it a capital
Nothing bad could ever happen to it
check.why: Jeremiah warned that Babylon would come. The Temple building alone would not save the city.

check.q: Why did Jeremiah wear a wooden yoke?
choices: To carry water to the Temple
To show that Judah would serve Babylon
check.why: Jeremiah 27 says he put a yoke on his neck as a sign that the nations would serve the king of Babylon.

check.q: What happened to Jeremiah for his message?
choices: He was beaten and put in a muddy pit
He was given a house in Babylon
check.why: Jeremiah 38 says officials lowered him into a pit with mud in it. He was pulled out later.

lessons.title: Far from Home: The Exile
lessons.mainIdea: In 586 BCE Babylon burned the Temple and took many people away; the text says they wept by the rivers of Babylon and did not forget Jerusalem.
reading: Jeremiah's warning came true. The book of 2 Kings, chapter 25, says the Babylonian army broke through the walls of Jerusalem. They burned the Temple that Solomon had built. They burned the palace and the houses. Historians date this to 586 BCE. Many people were marched away to Babylon.

Living far from home under a foreign king is called *exile*. The Hebrew word is galut. Psalm 137 gives the feeling. It says the people sat down by the rivers of Babylon and wept when they remembered Zion, another name for Jerusalem. Their captors asked them to sing. They asked how they could sing the LORD's song in a strange land.

The exile did not last forever. About fifty years later, a new king, Cyrus of Persia, let people go home and rebuild. But the exile changed Jewish life. Without a Temple, people gathered to pray and to read. Many historians say the synagogue and the habit of studying the text grew from this time. Every year on Tisha B'Av, Jewish communities fast and read Lamentations to remember the burned Temple.

words.d: living far from home because you were forced to leave; the Hebrew word is galut
another name for Jerusalem in the Tanakh, used in songs and prayers
the fast day when Jewish communities remember the destruction of the Temple
the king of Persia who, the text says, let the exiles go home to rebuild

look.title: From the Split to the Return
rows: Amos speaks in the north, about (BCE)
Cyrus lets the exiles return, about (BCE)
look.cite: 2 Kings 17 and 25; Ezra 1; dates as commonly given by historians
look.prompt: Put these events in order on a line. How many years passed between the burning of Jerusalem and the return?

check.q: What happened to Solomon's Temple in 586 BCE?
check.why: 2 Kings 25 says the Babylonian army burned the Temple. Historians date it to 586 BCE.

check.q: What does exile mean?
choices: Living far from home because you were forced to leave
check.why: Exile, galut in Hebrew, means being taken from your home to live in a foreign land.

check.q: Which psalm remembers weeping by the rivers of Babylon?
check.why: Psalm 137 begins with the people sitting by the rivers of Babylon and weeping for Zion.

review.q: What does the word navi mean?
review.why: Navi is the Hebrew word for prophet. Nevi'im, the Prophets, is the second part of the Tanakh.

review.q: Which prophet met the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel?
review.why: 1 Kings 18 tells of Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.

review.q: Which prophet picked up Elijah's cloak?
review.why: 2 Kings 2 says Elisha took up the mantle that fell from Elijah.

review.q: Which prophet was a shepherd from Tekoa who said justice should flow like water?
review.why: Amos 5:24 is the verse about justice like water. Amos was a shepherd from Tekoa.

review.q: What does Isaiah 2:4 say nations will do with their swords?
review.why: Isaiah 2:4 pictures swords becoming farm tools and nations not learning war anymore.

review.q: On which day is the book of Jonah read in the synagogue?
review.why: The whole book of Jonah is the afternoon haftarah on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.

review.q: Which empire burned Jerusalem in 586 BCE?
review.why: Babylon burned the Temple in 586 BCE. Assyria had taken the north in 722 BCE. Persia later let the exiles return.

choices: A cup of wine set for Elijah at the Passover Seder
A cup found in Jonah's fish
The cup used on Yom Kippur
review.why: Many Jewish families pour a cup for Elijah at the Seder and open the door, because Malachi says Elijah will return.
